claim: A rate-of-rise alarm warns of river surges earlier than a fixed level alarm.
data_label: open data: FOEN/BAFU 10-min and daily; simulated surges
stats: earlier than a fixed alarm, real surge
limit: No real glacial-lake outburst tested; only 12 real 10-min surges in 40 days. Not an official warning system.
alt: Dark chart. Top: a real river surge in the Weisse Lutschine on 25 October 2026, with a green rate-of-rise alarm line 1.7 hours before the red fixed-level alarm line. Bottom: simulated 5x surges, hours of earlier warning versus rise time.
post:
A glacial lake can empty in hours, and a level sensor downstream only raises its voice once the river is already high. I built a small open-source rate-of-rise alarm for exactly that case: it watches how fast the level climbs, not how high it is.

It combines a rate-of-rise rule, a CUSUM change detector, a simple travel-time estimate to points downstream, and a sampling rule that speeds up only while the water rises, to save battery on low-power sensors.

Measured numbers: on a real 10-minute surge in the Weisse Lutschine (25 October 2026, open FOEN/BAFU data) it fired 1.7 hours before a fixed level alarm. On 40 years of daily data from 14 glacier-fed gauges, dry-weather false alarms were 0.09 per station-year in the 2001-2020 test years. In simulation, adaptive sampling needed 62 percent fewer samples.

What is not verified: I found no open high-resolution record of a real glacial-lake outburst, so those surges are simulated. The real 10-minute evidence is small: 12 surges in 40 days at three stations. Rain floods also trigger the alarm, and at regulated stations with a daily release pattern it fires far too often. It is not an official warning system.

Would you trust a rate-based alarm over a level alarm at your site, and what would you want to see first?

Code: https://github.com/VB-Builds/lake-outburst-alarm
